advantages: Explains the unit as a sequence of problems solved rather than a list of products, which is how the 5-marker is framed.
Gives dated, checkable milestones (2008 whitepaper, 2009 genesis, 2014 yellow paper, 2015 mainnet, 2016 Fabric 1.0) so nothing is vague.
Ends with the business era, which is what the course title - Blockchain Business Models - is actually about.
limitations: A date-led history can turn into a list of years with no causal argument; the marks are in the 'because of' links.
History is low-yield compared with Terminologies and Types - 25 minutes, not 35 - so it should be read last.
Several dates are contested in the popular telling (the first Bitcoin transaction in January 2009, the Pizza transaction in May 2010), and an examiner may not care which you pick.
History of Blockchain.memoryTrick: **Trust in an owner → trust in economic cost → trust in code → trust in governance.** Three eras, one milestone each: Bitcoin 2008/09 (open), Ethereum 2014/15 (programmable), Fabric 2016 (governed).

examAnswer.question: Trace the development of blockchain from centralised databases to permissioned enterprise ledgers, naming the milestones in each era.
examAnswer.full:
A blockchain exists because a shared ledger needs a trusted keeper, and a trusted keeper can rewrite history - while two parties without a common database can each accept a different version of the same payment, which is the double-spending problem.

**Era 1 — the centralised era.** Ledgers were owned: a bank, a clearing house, a government registry. Trust came from the owner, reconciliation was manual, and the owner's rules decided which version of a payment counted.

**Era 2 — the open era, 2008-2009.** Hashcash (1992) had already priced a message by proof of computational work, and e-cash systems such as DigiCash (1995) attempted digital money but still needed an issuer. Bitcoin's whitepaper, posted in October 2008, removed the issuer: double spending is prevented because making a conflicting history requires redoing the proof of work of every block after it, so forgery costs more than honesty. The genesis block was mined in January 2009. Each block stores the hash of its predecessor, so history becomes tamper-evident rather than trusted.

**Era 3 — the programmable era, 2014-2015.** Ethereum's yellow paper (2014) and mainnet launch (July 2015) kept the hash-linked ledger but made it Turing-complete: rules could be deployed as smart contracts instead of hard-coded into every client. This is what made 'programmable money' a real phrase.

**Era 4 — the governed enterprise era, 2015 onwards.** Hyperledger Fabric 1.0 shipped in 2016 and Corda followed, moving the same machinery into networks of known organisations where consensus is a governance agreement and BFT voting rather than open mining. Tokenisation, DeFi and CBDCs added assets and regulation to the public side, while consortia such as TradeLens and we.trade added identity and privacy to the permissioned side.

**Conclusion.** Each era removed a different bottleneck: Bitcoin removed the trusted owner, Ethereum added programmability, permissioned chains added governance and legal accountability. The business payoff of the whole arc is that agreement between organisations that do not trust each other stops being a bilateral negotiation and becomes a shared record.

advantages: This is the highest-density topic in the unit: one 15-marker plus a 1-marker MCQ sit directly on it.
The definitions are reusable in every other answer - a well-stated block and nonce earn credit again in How blockchain works.
The node/wallet/address distinction is the single most common marking discriminator, so naming it explicitly protects several marks at once.
limitations: Definitions are easy to over-memorise and paraphrase badly; the exam wants the precise clause (20 bytes, 32 bytes, 2016 blocks), not the gist.
Ten terms is a lot of recall load for a 30-minute topic - if short of time, learn block, chain, nonce, node, wallet, address first.
The values (10-minute block time, 2016-block retarget) are Bitcoin's; permissioned chains differ, so do not present them as universal.
Terminologies in Blockchain.memoryTrick: **Block = body + header; header = prev-hash + Merkle root + time + difficulty + nonce.** Node keeps the ledger, wallet keeps the keys, address is the hash of the public key - 20 bytes to a 32-byte key.

examAnswer.question: Define the key terminologies of blockchain - block, chain, nonce, difficulty, block time, fork, node, wallet and address - and explain how they fit together.
examAnswer.full:
**Block.** A batch of transactions plus a header. The body carries the transactions; the header carries the commitments: the previous block's hash, the Merkle root of the transactions, a timestamp, the difficulty target and the nonce. The header is what gets hashed; the body is what the header commits to.

**Chain.** The sequence of blocks in which every block stores the hash of the block before it. Altering any historical block changes its hash and therefore every later hash, so history is tamper-evident rather than merely agreed.

**Nonce.** The 32-bit number in the header that the miner varies until the header's SHA-256 hash falls below the difficulty target. It is the entire search space of proof of work - not the block number, not the transaction count.

**Difficulty.** How hard the target is to satisfy, expressed as the number of leading zero bits required in a valid hash. It is retargeted every 2016 blocks, roughly two weeks, so that the block time stays near 600 seconds.

**Block time.** The average gap between consecutive blocks - about 10 minutes on Bitcoin, seconds on many permissioned chains. It is an average, not a guarantee.

**Fork.** A split of the chain into two competing branches at the same height. A soft fork is resolved by the branch with greater accumulated work; a hard fork by a coordinated protocol upgrade.

**Node.** A participant's machine that stores a copy of the ledger and independently validates and relays blocks and transactions. A full node validates every block; a light node checks only headers.

**Wallet.** Software that holds the user's keypair and signs transactions with it. The wallet holds keys, not coins - the coins are entries in the shared ledger, and the wallet holds the right to spend them.

**Address.** RIPEMD-160 applied to SHA-256 of the public key, giving 20 bytes (160 bits), printed as a 26-35 character Base58Check string. The public key itself is 32 bytes, or 64 hex characters.

**How they fit together.** A sender signs a transaction paying to an address. Validated transactions are collected into a block, whose Merkle root commits to them and whose header also commits to the previous block. The nonce is varied until the header hash satisfies the difficulty target, which is what lets the network agree on one ordering and one canonical chain. The full set of terminologies is therefore a single machine: key to address, address to payment, payment to block, block to chain.

advantages: A five-marker comparison with four named types is one of the most predictable questions on the paper.
The two-axis framing (permissioning x ownership) means the answer can be reconstructed from first principles if the table is forgotten.
Directly feeds the business-model framing of the course - each type is a governance model, not a technology.
The MCQ on a supply-chain consortium is won by anyone who has the permissioning/liability logic rather than a memorised list.
limitations: The 'private vs consortium' distinction is genuinely blurry in practice - the honest answer says the boundary is ownership of the rules and shared liability, not the word private.
Getting the trust source right (economics vs governance) is where most students lose a mark: they describe the type but not why the trust works.
Real deployments mix types; a pure public chain with permissioned side-channels is now common, so avoid presenting the four as clean boxes.
Types of Blockchain.memoryTrick: **Two axes: who writes, who owns.** Public = anyone writes, nobody owns, trust by economics. Private = one owner. Consortium = named members, shared liability. Hybrid = public settles, private keeps secrets.

examAnswer.question: Compare public, private, consortium and hybrid blockchains on permissioning, identity, consensus and governance, and say which type fits a vetted supply-chain consortium.
examAnswer.full:
The types differ on two axes. The first is permissioning - who may read and write the ledger. The second is ownership - who owns the rules and who bears liability for them. Once these are fixed, the trust source, the consensus mechanism and the governance arrangement follow automatically.

**Public chain (Bitcoin, Ethereum).** Anyone may read and write; there is no gatekeeper, so identity is pseudonymous and validation is permissionless. Because there is no gatekeeper, trust cannot come from an agreement, so it comes from economics: proof of work or proof of stake, and the cost of rewriting history. Governance is the protocol rules themselves, changed by node consensus. Reach is global and finality is economic, but throughput is low, writes are expensive and privacy is nil.

**Private chain.** One organisation owns the ledger, admits its members, and can validate with a single node or a small majority. Speed and privacy are excellent. The cost is the point of the technology: a single owner is exactly the trusted party blockchain was meant to remove, so a private chain usually saves little against one well-governed database.

**Consortium chain (Hyperledger Fabric, Corda, Quorum).** A group of known, KYC-ed legal entities jointly own the rules and share liability. Identity is named, so accountability is legal rather than economic. Consensus is voting-based - BFT, PBFT, Raft, or an ordering service in Fabric - because membership is known, so there is no need to burn energy. Governance is a council of member organisations. Blocks are seconds apart and privacy is strong.

**Hybrid chain.** A public layer carries the token and the settlement finality, while a private channel or permissioned side-chain carries confidential business data. The two layers settle against each other, so each keeps the property it needs.

**Trade-off in one line.** Public buys reach and economic finality at the cost of speed, cost and anonymity; permissioned buys speed, privacy and legal recourse at the cost of a closed membership and a smaller pool of trust.

**The supply-chain consortium is a consortium chain.** The participants are a known, vetted set of manufacturers, carriers and retailers who share the rules and share liability, they need named identities for regulatory reasons, and they want seconds-level blocks for goods in transit. Consensus is voting-based rather than mining-based because the members are already known to each other.

advantages: A short topic (20 minutes) that yields a full 5-marker by pairing domains with friction.
Every domain in the syllabus has a natural real-world example, so the answer can be concrete rather than generic.
The workflow-not-ledger framing is the mark that separates a 5 from a 10 - it shows business understanding, not technology.
limitations: Easy marks to waste on a sector list; pairing each domain with the problem it solves is what earns them.
Several real deployments in these domains have been scaled back or abandoned, so the answer should stay honest about when blockchain is the wrong tool.
No fixed list of domains is guaranteed - prepare at least two beyond the ones named so you can place whichever the paper chooses.
Applications of Blockchain.memoryTrick: **Ledger records, tokens/contracts enforce.** Applications = shared record between parties with no shared database. Payoff is measured in reconciliation hours and disputes avoided.

examAnswer.question: Discuss the real-time applications of blockchain, placing each named domain against the problem it solves.
examAnswer.full:
Every application worth building on a blockchain has the same shape: several organisations that do not share a trusted database need to agree on one record. If only one organisation holds the record, a database is the cheaper and better answer.

**The application is the workflow, not the ledger.** The ledger records the state transition; a token or a smart contract enforces the condition and triggers whatever happens next. Putting records on a chain without an enforcing contract is not an application.

**Cross-border payments.** Today a payment crosses 2-4 correspondent banks, each taking a cut and a day. A shared ledger makes the payment itself the common record, removing correspondent fees and settlement days.

**Supply chain.** Provenance without a central auditor: each handoff is written by the participants themselves and cannot be quietly edited afterwards, so a recalled or counterfeit part can be traced to its origin.

**Land registry.** One ownership record instead of duplicate titles held in several offices, which cuts disputes over who owns what and enables instant transfer.

**Healthcare.** Records the patient holds and carries across providers without re-papering, with access to each record controlled per record and the data itself typically kept off-chain with only hashes or consent on the ledger.

**Digital identity.** Credentials the citizen holds and reuses, so each service verifies once rather than every service re-papering from scratch.

**Trade finance.** Bills of lading, letters of credit and insurance whose state is shared by all parties, removing the reconciliation and the fraud that goes with it.

**How the business case is measured.** In reconciliation hours removed, disputes avoided, settlement days cut and correspondent fees eliminated - not in the word decentralisation.

**The honest limit.** A blockchain is the wrong answer where one party already holds the trusted record, where the volume is low enough for a shared database, or where the law will not accept the ledger's record as evidence.

advantages: The unit's flagship 15-marker, and the seven-step path (sign, broadcast, validate, order, aggregate, agree, append) is the answer body - it maps one mark per step.
Every step has a distinct failure mode, so the answer can explain why each step exists rather than listing labels.
The tamper-history question has a precise, high-scoring answer: every block from the tampered one to the tip must be re-hashed and re-mined.
The finality numbers (6 confirmations, about 60 minutes, (1/2)^6 near 1.6%) are concrete and easy marks.
limitations: The longest topic in the unit (35 minutes) and the easiest to over-read; the mechanism list alone answers the paper.
Mining-based steps (nonce, difficulty, mempool, fee rate) belong to Bitcoin-style chains; a permissioned chain substitutes voting and an ordering service - say which chain you are describing.
Order and consensus are easy to conflate; ordering is only a proposal in the mempool, consensus is what makes it agreed.
Do not let the finality paragraph swallow the answer - it is the last 2 marks, not the whole 15.
How blockchain works.memoryTrick: **Sign → Broadcast → Validate → Order → Aggregate → Agree → Append.** Signing proves who, validation proves what, consensus proves in which order. Tamper one old block and you redo every block from there to the tip.

examAnswer.question: Trace the lifecycle of a transaction in a blockchain from signing through broadcast, validation, block assembly, consensus and appending, and explain what a tampered historical transaction forces the network to redo.
examAnswer.full:
**1. Sign.** The sender's wallet constructs the transaction and signs it with the private key (ECDSA over SHA-256). The signature proves intent and ownership of the input; the recipient's address is the hash of the public key. Signing proves who, and nothing else.

**2. Broadcast.** The signed transaction is pushed to the sender's peers, which relay it across the peer-to-peer network until it reaches the mempool of every node. There is no central inbox.

**3. Validate.** Each node independently checks the transaction is well formed and affordable: the signature verifies against the referenced public key, the inputs have not already been spent, the output sum does not exceed the input sum, and the fee clears the mempool minimum. Failing nodes drop it and it never propagates further.

**4. Order.** Valid transactions sit in the mempool, ordered by fee rate on Bitcoin or by an ordering service in Fabric. This ordering is a proposal, not an agreement - and it is exactly where a double spend would sit, two conflicting versions of the same spend waiting to be placed.

**5. Aggregate.** The ordered transactions form the block body. Their hashes are combined into a Merkle root, a single hash committing to every transaction in the body. The header then carries the previous block's hash, the Merkle root, a timestamp, the difficulty target and the nonce.

**6. Agree (consensus).** The miner varies the nonce until SHA-256 of the header is below the target - proof of work - or, on a permissioned chain, the validator set reaches a voting quorum under BFT. The branch with the greater accumulated work is declared canonical and the other is orphaned. Consensus is what defeats the double spend: only one version of a conflicting spend survives.

**7. Append.** The new block is broadcast; every node verifies the hash link to the previous block and stores it, and the chain grows by one. The block that contained the transaction is one confirmation deep; confidence grows with every block on top.

**What a tampered historical transaction forces the network to redo.** Because every block commits to the hash of the one before it, editing a transaction inside an old block changes that block's hash, which changes the header of the next block, and so on to the tip. The network must therefore recompute the hash and the proof of work of every block from the tampered block onwards - the block where the tamper sits plus every block after it - and rebuild the unspent-output set, because the spend that was reversed must be removed and re-spent. On Bitcoin, that means redoing the work of the honest network from that height to the tip, which is why a rewrite is technically possible but economically irrational: an attacker must out-spend all the honest work done since that block. This is why the chain is append-only in practice rather than by law.

**Finality is empirical, not mathematical.** Bitcoin users accept about 6 confirmations, roughly 60 minutes at a 10 minute block time, and the chance of a fork overtaking that falls roughly as (1/2)^6, about 1.6%. Permissioned chains with voting consensus reach finality in seconds, but their finality is a governance guarantee rather than an economic one.

advantages: A 5-marker listing question is the cheapest high-value answer in the unit, provided each ingredient is paired with the attack it removes.
The 'each ingredient defeats one attack' structure means the list cannot be blurred - it is checkable.
It supplies the vocabulary (hash, signature, keypair, consensus, timestamp, mining) reused across every other topic in the unit.
The final point - the ingredients only work in combination - is the difference between a 5 and a 10.
limitations: A bare list of six ingredients is a memorisation task; the attack-to-ingredient mapping is what earns the marks.
Mining is the Sybil defence of open chains only; in permissioned chains the equivalent is leader election with Sybil-resistant identity, so say which chain you mean.
Do not over-claim confidentiality - hashing and signing provide integrity and authenticity, and the ledger is public.
The list does not include business-rule validation, which is what smart contracts add - a validly signed nonsense transaction is still nonsense until code checks it.
Ingredients of Blockchain.memoryTrick: **Hash beats tampering, signature beats forgery, keys beat impersonation, replication beats single-point failure, consensus beats conflicting history, timestamp beats backdating, mining beats Sybil.**

examAnswer.question: List the ingredients of a blockchain and explain the role each one plays.
examAnswer.full:
A blockchain is assembled from seven ingredients, and each one removes exactly one attack on the shared record.

**1. Hash function (SHA-256).** Maps any input to a fixed 256-bit digest. Each block's header stores the previous block's hash and the Merkle root of its own transactions, so history becomes tamper-evident: a one-bit edit changes the whole digest and breaks every later link. This defeats tampering.

**2. Digital signature.** The sender signs with the private key; anyone verifies with the public key. It proves the holder of the key authorised that specific transaction, and cannot be forged or repudiated. It defeats forgery - and note it gives authenticity and non-repudiation, not confidentiality.

**3. Asymmetric key pairs.** The private key signs, the public key verifies, and the address is a hash of the public key (RIPEMD-160 of SHA-256, 20 bytes). Identity is self-issued, so there is no account issuance and no impersonation without the key.

**4. Distributed ledger and peer-to-peer network.** Every node keeps its own copy, so there is no single point of failure and no owner who can suppress or censor a record.

**5. Consensus mechanism.** Proof of work (economic, open chains) or BFT voting (permissioned chains) selects one canonical ordering of transactions. This is what defeats the double-spending problem and conflicting histories: only one version of a conflicting spend survives.

**6. Timestamp.** The creation time in the header bounds how far back a rewrite could have been prepared and prevents records being backdated.

**7. Mining, or its permissioned equivalent.** Mining makes influence cost computational resources, which is the Sybil defence - an entity flooding the network with a thousand fake identities buys no extra weight. In a permissioned chain the equivalent is leader election or round-robin with Sybil-resistant identity.

**The parts only work together.** Each ingredient closes one hole, but each depends on the others. A signature without an ordering rule merely signs messages nobody has agreed to place in order. A hash chain without consensus is just a chain the nodes disagree about. And none of the seven is a business-rule check - a validly signed but nonsensical transaction still needs code, which is what smart contracts add.
